Phospholipases are a group of enzymes which break down phospholipids in membranes. There are two main classes of these enzymes, those that act on glycerophospholipids and those that act on sphingomyelin. Of the glycerophospholipid phospholipases, there are three main sub-classes; the PLA2s (phospholipase A2), PLCs (phospholipase C) and PTAs (phospholipase A1).  Phospholipase A2 - PLA2 is the only enzyme which can release arachidonic acid from cell membranes, therefore is the correct answer. It is also known as cytosolic PLA2 because it resides in the cytosol of cells. Other members of the PLA2 family include calcium dependent PLA2 and secretory PLA2. These other members do not have a role in prostaglandin production.  Phospholipase B1 - PLB1 is an incorrect name for an enzyme.  Phospholipase C is an incorrect class of enzyme.  Phospholipase A1 - PLA1 is an incorrect name for an enzyme. This enzyme is actually part of the phospholipase A2 family and catalyses the release of palmitoyl groups from phospholipids. It is found in liver and brain and has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease.  Sources: "The Cellular Environment" and "Biochemistry" both by Squire. Also Wikipedia. A - incorrect as the first codon always is AUG and therefore the anticodons are UAGB - incorrect as the third codon in the anticodon is wrongC - incorrect as the second codon in the anticodon is wrongD - incorrect as the fourth codon in the anticodon is wrongE - correct! This is how we remember it - UAGC is the start codon, and GUC is the stop codon. Therefore the first amino acid's anticodon will be UAC. After this the other amino acids are coded by their respective codons. For example, arginine is coded by AGG (the third codon) and its anticodon would be CGA. We then go down the list until we get to the next stop codon. This will code for tyrosine, which is TAC. We then continue down the list until proline which is CCU. Then we hit the start codon again. It goes: UAC, AGG, TAC, CCU, ACG, GCU, UGG, UGA, GAA, GAG, GUC. We then go back down the list again until we find another stop codon. This will code for leucine which is UUA. We then continue down the list until phenylalanine which is UUU. We then go back up the list until serine which is UCA. And so on... Hopefully this makes sense! I found it easier to learn the anticodons for the first few amino acids and then go through the list once and try to work out the others yourself. Also, I found it helpful to know that the stop codon is UGA and that it doesn't have an anticodon. After childbirth, the spiral arteries contract again and cause the endometrium to slough off and bleed. The endometrial glands regress. Myosin light chain kinase usually phosphorylates the myosin light chain, binding it to actin and allowing contraction of cardiac muscle cells. However when myosin light chain kinase is dephosphorylated by myosin phosphatase, the myosin light chain is no longer bound to actin and contraction cannot occur, therefore leading to vasodilation. This inhibits myosin light chain kinase activity. The myosin light chain phosphatase is always present but normally inactive. When myosin light chain kinase is inhibited, myosin phosphatase becomes active and dephosphorylates the myosin light chain, therefore preventing contraction of the cardiomyocyte. Metabolic acidosis is caused by an increase in HCO3- or decrease in pH due to increased acid production, such as diabetes ketoacidosis. This could be caused by the kidneys excreting too much H+ in response to a low pH (renal tubular acidosis), or vomiting too much (resulting in loss of stomach acid). Erb-Duchenne palsy causes loss of muscle innervation from C5 and below. This would result in weakness of the arm as well as wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist and the digits). It would also cause Horner's syndrome which is characterised by ptosis, anhidrosis and erythroderma. Klumpke paralysis is similar to Erb- Duchenne palsy except it occurs due to injury at C6 and C7 levels. This results in weakness of wrist extension, flexion of the middle finger, and hyperextension of the elbow. However, unlike Erb-Duchenne palsy, it does not affect the muscles supplying the shoulder so there is no winged scapula or weakness of the upper extremity. Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve as it travels through the carpal tunnel at the wrist. Symptoms include numbness, tingling, and pain that radiates to the forearm. Claw hand is a permanent flexion of the distal interphalangeal joints which is caused by damage to the ulnar nerve. It usually occurs proximally in the cubital fossa or in Guyon's canal at the base of the hand. Damage to the anterior interosseus nerve can also result in claw hand.
